scenarios.title: Troubleshooting: Azure RBAC: Roles, Scopes, and Least Privilege
scenarios.situation: After a change involving azure rbac: roles, scopes, and least privilege, users report degraded behavior. Reviewing the implementation, you find the team fell into a known trap: Owner at subscription scope for daily work — Contributor or narrower suffices. Background: RBAC = role definition (permissions) + assignment (who) + scope (where: management group → subscription → resource group → resource). Deny assignments override.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely root cause, and what is the best next step?
choices: Remediate the root cause: RBAC = role definition (permissions) + assignment (who) + scope (where: management group → subscription → resource group → resource). Deny assignments override. Then verify with the checks from training.
Treat the symptom: confusing control-plane (manage vm) with data-plane (read blobs) — storage blob data contributor is separate from contributor.
Increase capacity — bigger resources fix most issues
Roll back the monitoring — alerts are the problem, not the system
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The observed trap (Owner at subscription scope for daily work — Contributor or narrower suffices.) directly explains the degradation: RBAC = role definition (permissions) + assignment (who) + scope (where: management group → subscription → resource group → resource). Deny assignments override. Built-in roles: Owner, Contributor, Reader, User Access Administrator; plus granular ones (VM Contributor, Storage Blob Data Contributor). Data-plane vs control-plane actions differ. The distractors treat symptoms, add cost without diagnosis, or remove visibility.
scenarios.hint: Connect the observed trap to the lesson's first key concept.
objectives: Diagnose Azure RBAC: Roles, Scopes, and Least Privilege failures
evidence: Degradation began after the change; implementation shows: Owner at subscription scope for daily work — Contributor or narrower suffices.

lessons.title: Storage — Core concepts
concepts: Storage redundancy: the storage account firewall (Firewalls and virtual networks) defaults to deny and whitelists VNets (via service endpoints/private endpoints) and IP ranges. Storage Explorer is fine for small interactive work but not 10 TB bulk migration.
ZRS synchronously replicates three copies across availability zones in the primary region — surviving a datacenter loss without paying for a second region.
Access tiers: shared access signatures grant constrained, time-limited access (permissions, IP, expiry) without exposing account keys.
Lifecycle management policies automate tier transitions by age — e.g., Hot→Cool after 30 days, →Archive after 180 — so nobody does it manually.
Least-privilege access: a service SAS on the container with write-only for 48 hours is the least-privilege answer; keys and RBAC are far too broad.

example.code: azcopy copy 'D:\shares\*' 'https://staccount.blob.core.windows.net/archive<SAS>' --recursive --overwrite=ifSourceNewer
example.walkthrough: AzCopy is the purpose-built high-performance copy tool (azcopy copy/sync), multi-threaded with automatic resume on failure. Storage Explorer is fine for small interactive work but not 10 TB bulk migration.

Availability sets provide fault/update domain spread but no scaling or identical-image management.

Autoscale: VMSS manages identical VMs as a set with autoscale based on metrics (CPU, queue length), plus rolling upgrades.

VNet peering: a-to-C needs its own peering (or a hub VNet with routing/NVA). Private endpoints bring the PaaS service into your VNet with a private IP (resolving via private DNS zone), eliminating public endpoint exposure.
ExpressRoute vs VPN: S2S VPN rides the public internet with variable throughput; peering only connects Azure VNets.
User-defined routes override Azure's default system routes — the mechanism behind forced tunneling and NVA traffic inspection.

lessons.title: Monitoring — Core concepts

Metric alert rules evaluate platform/guest metrics on a frequency and fire action groups (email, SMS, webhooks, Logic Apps).

Azure Monitor data: disk space is a guest metric (via Azure Monitor Agent); the action group delivers the notification. Service Health reports Azure platform incidents and planned maintenance per region — the first stop when many resources fail together with no config change.
KQL pipelines: filter with where, aggregate with summarize ... by, rank with top.
Alert rules: network Watcher's IP flow verify simulates a packet against NSG rules, and 'next hop' reveals the effective route (system, UDR, or peering).

example.code: TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, ResultType, IPAddress

lessons.title: Azure Administrator — Core concepts
concepts: Resource groups are logical containers for lifecycle management: ARM deploys to a resource group in Incremental mode (default, non-destructive) or Complete mode (deletes anything not in the template). Choose the mode deliberately.
Virtual networks segment traffic into subnets; NSGs filter at subnet and NIC level with priority-ordered rules where lower numbers win and an explicit deny anywhere in the path drops the packet.

Storage accounts offer redundancy tiers matched to failure scope: LRS (one datacenter), ZRS (zones in one region), GRS/RA-GRS (secondary region). Access tiers Hot, Cool, and Archive trade retrieval cost for storage cost.
Virtual machines gain resilience from availability sets (fault/update domains within a datacenter) or availability zones (separate datacenters); managed disks decouple storage lifecycle from the VM.

Entra ID is the identity plane: users and groups live in a tenant, and RBAC assignments pair a role definition with a scope. Least privilege means the narrowest role at the narrowest scope — administrative units narrow user scope.
Azure Policy and resource locks are guardrails: policy denies or audits non-compliant deployments, while CanNotDelete and ReadOnly locks protect resources from accidental change regardless of RBAC.

example.code:
az group create --name rg-az104 --location eastus
az network vnet create --resource-group rg-az104 --name vnet-app \
  --address-prefix 10.1.0.0/16 --subnet-name web --subnet-prefix 10.1.1.0/24
az network nsg create --resource-group rg-az104 --name nsg-web
az network nsg rule create --resource-group rg-az104 --nsg-name nsg-web \
  --name Allow-HTTPS --priority 100 --destination-port-ranges 443 --access Allow
example.walkthrough: Create a resource group, then a VNet with one subnet, then an NSG with a single HTTPS allow rule at priority 100. Note the defaults you did not set: the VNet gets default allow-VNet and deny-all inbound rules, and your rule slots into the priority order.

pitfalls: Common trap: assuming a higher-priority-number rule wins — lower numbers are evaluated first, and the first match decides.
Common trap: using Complete deployment mode on a shared resource group and deleting resources the template never mentioned.
Common trap: picking LRS or ZRS when the requirement is surviving a regional outage — only GRS/RA-GRS replicate to a second region.
Common trap: troubleshooting only the NSG while a UDR or Azure Firewall silently drops the traffic on another layer.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems

Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence

lessons.title: Hybrid Identity: Entra Connect and Cloud Sync
concepts: Entra Connect Sync replicates on-prem AD to Entra ID: PHS (password hash sync, simplest, leaked-credential detection), PTA (pass-through, passwords stay on-prem), Federation (AD FS, most complex).
PHS is the default recommendation: synced hashes enable seamless SSO + leaked credential reports; PTA suits security policies forbidding cloud password storage.
Cloud Sync is the lightweight agent alternative for multi-forest or simple topologies — no SQL, auto-updates, but fewer customization options.
Seamless SSO + PHS gives users silent sign-in on domain machines; monitor sync health in Entra Connect Health.

example.code:
# Verify sync status
Get-MgOrganization | Select -ExpandProperty OnPremisesSyncEnabled
# Force delta sync
Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta
example.walkthrough: PHS vs PTA vs Federation is a classic exam decision: default PHS unless policy forbids it (PTA) or you need claims customization (Federation). Know the tradeoff table cold.

pitfalls: Choosing AD FS when PHS meets requirements — unnecessary complexity is penalized.
Forgetting staging mode for the second sync server — two active export servers corrupt data.
Ignoring sync errors in Connect Health — users silently stop provisioning.
lessons.try_it: Map PHS/PTA/Federation to three org profiles and justify each choice.

lessons.title: Microsoft Entra ID: Tenants, Users, and Groups
concepts: Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) is the identity plane: tenants hold users, groups, and app registrations; one tenant per organization typically.
User types: cloud-only, synchronized (Entra Connect/Cloud Sync), guest (B2B). Groups: security (access) vs Microsoft 365 (collaboration); dynamic groups use attribute rules.
Licenses gate features: Free vs P1 (Conditional Access, dynamic groups) vs P2 (Identity Protection, PIM, Access Reviews).
App registrations use OAuth2/OIDC: service principals are the local instance of an app in each tenant; managed identities are auto-managed service principals for Azure resources.

example.code:
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'Group.ReadWrite.All'
New-MgGroup -DisplayName 'Prod-Admins' -MailEnabled:$false `
  -SecurityEnabled:$true -MailNickname 'prodadmins'
# dynamic rule: user.department -eq 'Engineering'
example.walkthrough: Groups drive access: assign RBAC roles to groups, not users. Exam pattern: 'manage access at scale' → security groups + RBAC, dynamic membership for auto-onboarding.

pitfalls: Assigning roles to individual users instead of groups — unmanageable and fails governance questions.
Using M365 groups where security groups are needed — different purposes, different behaviors.
Forgetting P1/P2 licensing for Conditional Access and PIM — features silently unavailable.
lessons.try_it: Create a dynamic security group with a department rule and verify auto-membership.

lessons.title: Conditional Access: Zero-Trust Policy Engine
concepts: CA policies are if-then: signals (user, device, location, risk, app) → grant controls (require MFA, compliant device, block). All policies evaluated; most restrictive grant wins on conflict.
Named locations define trusted IPs; risk policies use Identity Protection signals (unfamiliar sign-in, leaked credentials).
Always test in Report-only mode first, exclude break-glass accounts, and roll out gradually — a bad CA policy locks out the org.
Filters for devices and authentication strengths (FIDO2 vs SMS) give granular control beyond allow/block.

example.code:
# Report-only first, then enable
New-MgIdentityConditionalAccessPolicy -DisplayName 'MFA for admins' `
  -State 'enabledForReportingButNotEnforced' `
  -Conditions @{ Users=@{ IncludeRoles=@('Global Administrator') }; Applications=@{ IncludeApplications=@('All') } } `
  -GrantControls @{ Operator='OR'; BuiltInControls=@('mfa') }
example.walkthrough: Report-only → review sign-in logs → enforce. Break-glass accounts excluded from every policy. This rollout discipline is what exam scenarios test.

pitfalls: Enforcing without report-only testing — self-inflicted lockout is the classic failure.
No break-glass exclusions — emergency access must bypass CA.
Targeting 'All users' including service accounts — scope policies precisely.
lessons.try_it: Build a CA policy requiring compliant devices for SharePoint, in report-only mode.

lessons.title: Hybrid Networking: VPN Gateway and ExpressRoute
concepts: VPN Gateway: IPsec S2S (policy/route-based), P2S (per-user, OpenVPN/IKEv2), VNet-to-VNet; active-active for 99.95% SLA; BGP for dynamic routing.
ExpressRoute: private dedicated circuit (50Mbps–100Gbps), Global Reach, FastPath; needs provider + weeks lead time; SKUs standard/premium.
Coexistence: ER primary + VPN backup over the internet; connection monitor verifies paths.
Virtual WAN: managed hub-and-spoke for many branches/VNets with automated routing.

example.code:
az network vnet-gateway create -g prod-rg -n hub-gw --vnet hub-vnet \
  --public-ip gw-pip --gateway-type Vpn --vpn-type RouteBased --sku VpnGw2 --enable-bgp
example.walkthrough: RouteBased + BGP = dynamic failover. 'Resilient hybrid' → ER + S2S VPN backup, BGP preferring ER.

pitfalls: PolicyBased VPN for multi-site — route-based + BGP is the flexible answer.
Single tunnel/instance VPN gateway — active-active for SLA.
Forgetting gateway subnet sizing (/27+) and that it must be named GatewaySubnet.
lessons.try_it: Configure BGP peering on a VPN gateway and verify learned routes.

lessons.title: Backup and Site Recovery
concepts: Recovery Services vaults: VM backup (snapshot-based, 15-min–daily), Azure Files, SQL; backup policies + retention; soft delete + MFA delete protection.
Site Recovery: replicate VMs to another region (RPO minutes), failover/failback runbooks, non-disruptive test failovers.
Backup Center: central governance across vaults; immutable vaults block deletion for ransomware resilience.
3-2-1: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 offsite — GRS vault storage is the offsite.

example.code:
az backup protection enable-for-vm --resource-group prod-rg --vault-name prod-vault \
  --vm web1 --policy-name DailyPolicy
# test failover without impact:
# Site Recovery > Test Failover > isolated VNet
example.walkthrough: Backup for data loss, Site Recovery for region loss — different tools, both needed. 'Test DR without downtime' → test failover to isolated network.

pitfalls: Backup without soft delete — ransomware deletes backups too; enable soft delete + immutable vaults.
Never testing failover — untested DR is not DR; schedule test failovers.
ZRS-only thinking for regional events — GRS vault storage for true offsite.
lessons.try_it: Run a test failover of a VM to an isolated VNet and verify.

lessons.title: Storage Accounts: Kinds, Tiers, and Redundancy
concepts: Kinds: StorageV2 (general), BlockBlobStorage (premium block), FileStorage (premium files), BlobStorage (legacy). Performance: Standard vs Premium.
Redundancy: LRS (3 copies, 1 datacenter), ZRS (3 AZs), GRS (paired region), GZRS (both), RA-GRS (read access to secondary).
Tiers: Hot, Cool (30d+), Cold (90d+), Archive (rehydrate hours); lifecycle policies automate transitions; blob versioning + soft delete protect.
Secure transfer required (TLS), shared key vs Entra auth, private endpoints for VNet-only access.

example.code:
az storage account create -n stprod001 -g prod-rg -l eastus \
  --sku Standard_GZRS --kind StorageV2 --https-only true \
  --allow-blob-public-access false --min-tls-version TLS1_2
example.walkthrough: GZRS + no public access + TLS1.2 = the secure default. 'Survive regional outage with read access' → RA-GZRS.

pitfalls: LRS for critical data — single datacenter failure loses it; ZRS minimum for prod.
Public blob access left on — disable at account level unless intentionally public.
No lifecycle policy — hot-tier bills pile up on cold data.
lessons.try_it: Set a lifecycle rule: cool at 30 days, archive at 90, and verify with metrics.

lessons.title: Azure SQL: Database, Managed Instance, and Elastic Pools
concepts: SQL Database (PaaS, serverless vCore or DTU), Managed Instance (near-100% on-prem parity, VNet), SQL on VMs (full control).
HA: zone-redundant, auto-failover groups for region DR; backups: 7–35 day PITR, long-term retention to vaults.
Elastic pools share DTUs/vCores across many DBs (SaaS multi-tenant); hyperscale for 100TB+ with instant scaling.
Security: Entra auth, TDE, Always Encrypted, Defender for SQL (vulnerability assessment), private endpoint.

example.code:
az sql db create -g prod-rg -s prod-sql -n orders \
  --service-objective GP_Gen5_4 --zone-redundant true --backup-storage-redundancy Zone
az sql failover-group create --name fog --server prod-sql --partner-server dr-sql \
  -g prod-rg --failover-policy Automatic --grace-period 60
example.walkthrough: Zone-redundant + failover group = survive AZ and region events. 'SaaS with 200 tenants' → elastic pools.

pitfalls: DTU model for variable workloads — vCore serverless scales and often costs less.
No failover group for regional DR — zone redundancy does not cover regions.
SQL auth only — enable Entra auth and disable SQL auth where possible.
lessons.try_it: Set up a failover group and perform a planned failover.

lessons.title: Azure Monitor: Metrics, Logs, and Alerts
concepts: Metrics (platform, near-real-time) vs Logs (Log Analytics workspaces, KQL queries); diagnostic settings route both to destinations.
Alerts: metric, log (KQL), activity log; action groups (email/SMS/webhook/runbook); alert processing rules suppress/route.
Application Insights: APM for apps (requests, dependencies, exceptions); VM insights + Container insights for infra.
Change Analysis and Service Health complete the observability picture for incident response.

example.code:
// KQL: top failing dependencies, last hour
dependencies
| where timestamp > ago(1h) and success == false
| summarize failures=count() by target, type
| top 10 by failures
example.walkthrough: KQL is the exam's log-analysis language: filter → summarize → render. 'Find top errors' → App Insights/Logs + KQL.

pitfalls: No diagnostic settings — platform logs vanish; enable at creation via Policy.
Alerting on logs without aggregation — noisy; use metric alerts where possible.
Action groups missing — alerts fire into the void.
lessons.try_it: Write a KQL query finding the top 5 failed requests by operation name.

lessons.title: AKS: Managed Kubernetes
concepts: Control plane managed free; you pay for node pools (system + user). CNI choices: Azure CNI (VNet-integrated IPs) vs kubenet (simpler, NAT).
Workload identity (federated credentials) gives pods Entra identities — no secrets; Azure Key Vault CSI driver mounts secrets as volumes.
Ingress via Application Gateway (AGIC) or NGINX; autoscaling via HPA + cluster autoscaler; upgrade channels automate patching.
Defender for Containers scans images; Azure Policy for Kubernetes enforces guardrails (e.g., no privileged pods).

example.code:
az aks create -g prod-rg -n prodaks --node-count 3 --zones 1 2 3 \
  --network-plugin azure --enable-workload-identity --enable-oidc-issuer \
  --enable-addons monitoring,azure-keyvault-secrets-provider
example.walkthrough: Zone-spread nodes + workload identity + Key Vault CSI = secure baseline. 'Run microservices at scale' → AKS with these addons.

pitfalls: kubenet IP exhaustion at scale — Azure CNI with proper subnet sizing for large clusters.
Secrets as env vars from Key Vault — use the CSI driver for rotation-aware mounts.
No upgrade channel — clusters drift out of support; set patch/node-image channels.
lessons.try_it: Enable workload identity and have a pod read a Key Vault secret with no credentials.

lessons.title: App Service: PaaS Web Hosting
concepts: App Service plans define compute (Free→Premium v3, isolated ASE for VNet); apps deploy via zip/GitHub/Actions with slots.
Deployment slots: stage in staging, warm up, swap with zero downtime; auto-swap for CI/CD; slot-specific settings (connection strings).
Scale: manual, autoscale rules, or per-app scaling; Always On for non-free tiers; VNet integration for private backends.
Diagnostics: app logs, Kudu console, Application Insights integration; backup/restore built in.

example.code:
az webapp create -g prod-rg -p prod-plan -n myapp --runtime 'PYTHON|3.11'
az webapp deployment slot create -g prod-rg -n myapp --slot staging
az webapp deployment slot swap -g prod-rg -n myapp --slot staging
example.walkthrough: Deploy to staging → verify → swap. Traffic switches instantly with warmed instances. 'Zero-downtime deploys' → deployment slots.

pitfalls: Deploying straight to production — slots exist precisely to avoid this.
Free/Shared tier for prod — no SLA, no Always On, CPU quotas.
Secrets in app settings plaintext — use Key Vault references.
lessons.try_it: Set up staging slot with auto-swap after CI passes.

lessons.title: Azure Functions: Serverless Compute
concepts: Plans: Consumption (pay-per-execution, 10-min max), Premium (VNet, longer, pre-warmed), Dedicated (App Service plan).
Triggers: HTTP, Timer, Queue/Blob/Event Hub; bindings declare inputs/outputs — less boilerplate code.
Durable Functions orchestrate stateful workflows (chaining, fan-out, human interaction) with replay semantics.
Cold starts mitigated by Premium plan pre-warmed instances; Application Insights built in.

example.code:
func new --name OrderProcessor --template 'QueueTrigger'
# function.json bindings: queue input, table output -- no SDK code needed
az functionapp create -g prod-rg -n orders-fn --consumption-plan-location eastus \
  --runtime python --runtime-version 3.11 --functions-version 4
example.walkthrough: Trigger + bindings = event-driven without plumbing. 'Process queue messages serverless' → Queue trigger + output binding.

pitfalls: Consumption plan for VNet-restricted resources — needs Premium/Dedicated.
Long orchestration in one function — Durable Functions handles stateful workflows.
No idempotency on queue triggers — poison messages need DLQ handling.
lessons.try_it: Build a Durable Function that fans out to 10 activities and aggregates.

lessons.title: Container Apps: Serverless Containers
concepts: Managed Kubernetes-based hosting without cluster ops: containers scale to zero on HTTP/events (KEDA scalers).
Revisions: immutable snapshots with traffic splitting (blue/green, canary) built in.
Environments provide the VNet boundary; Dapr sidecars for pub/sub, state, service invocation.
Use for microservices that need K8s semantics without AKS operations.

example.code:
az containerapp create -g rg -n api --environment env \
  --image myreg.azurecr.io/api:v3 --target-port 8080 --ingress external \
  --min-replicas 0 --max-replicas 10 --scale-rule-name http --scale-rule-type http
example.walkthrough: Image → revision; traffic splits across revisions for safe deploys. 'K8s without the cluster' → Container Apps.

pitfalls: Expecting full K8s API — it is K8s-powered, not K8s-exposed.
No VNet environment for private workloads — default is public ingress.
Single revision strategy — traffic splitting is the safe-deploy mechanism.
lessons.try_it: Deploy two revisions and split traffic 90/10.

lessons.title: Static Web Apps: Global Frontends
concepts: Globally distributed static hosting + managed API (Functions) with staging environments per PR.
Built-in CI/CD from GitHub/ADO; custom domains with free managed certs; auth via Entra/GitHub/Twitter.
Routing config (staticwebapp.config.json): rewrites, headers, auth rules, response overrides.
Use for SPAs/JAMstack with serverless APIs; not for heavy SSR.

example.walkthrough: Push → preview environment per PR; merge → production. 'Frontend with preview deploys' → Static Web Apps.

pitfalls: API on the free tier for production — usage limits bite.
No routing config — auth rules and SPA fallback need the config file.
Secrets in the frontend bundle — APIs hold secrets, never the client.
lessons.try_it: Add an auth rule protecting /admin in the config.

lessons.title: API Management: Gateway Governance
concepts: Fronts APIs with policies: rate limiting, quotas, JWT validation, transformation, caching — per product/subscription.
Products bundle APIs; subscriptions issue keys; developer portal for discovery.
VNet integration (Premium/Standard v2) for private backends; self-hosted gateway for hybrid.
Policies are XML; version sets and revisions manage API evolution.

example.code:
<policies>
  <inbound>
    <rate-limit calls="100" renewal-period="60" />
    <validate-jwt header-name="Authorization">
      <openid-config url="https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tid}/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration" />
    </validate-jwt>
  </inbound>
</policies>
example.walkthrough: Import the API, attach the policy, publish the product. 'One gateway, many APIs, per-team quotas' → APIM.

pitfalls: No rate limiting — one consumer can starve the backend.
Keys without products — subscriptions need product scoping.
Public APIM with private backends but no VNet — traffic hairpins the internet.
lessons.try_it: Add a rate-limit + JWT policy to a test API.

lessons.title: Cosmos DB: Globally Distributed NoSQL
concepts: Multi-model (NoSQL, Mongo, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table); RU/s throughput (autoscale/serverless); 5 consistency levels (strong → eventual).
Global distribution: single write region or multi-region writes; <10ms reads/writes at 99.999% SLA with multi-region.
Partition key choice is everything: high cardinality, even distribution; change feed for CDC patterns.
Backup: continuous 30-day PITR; analytical store for HTAP with Synapse.

example.code:
az cosmosdb create -g prod-rg -n prod-cosmos --kind GlobalDocumentDB \
  --locations regionName=eastus failoverPriority=0 --locations regionName=westus failoverPriority=1 \
  --default-consistency-level Session
example.walkthrough: Session consistency + autoscale RU/s is the default right answer. 'Global app, low latency writes' → multi-region writes.

pitfalls: Bad partition key (e.g., status with 3 values) — hot partitions and throttling.
Strong consistency globally — latency/cost pain; session/eventual usually suffice.
Provisioned RU/s for spiky workloads — autoscale or serverless instead.
lessons.try_it: Load test with a good vs bad partition key and compare throttling.

lessons.title: Azure RBAC: Roles, Scopes, and Least Privilege
concepts: RBAC = role definition (permissions) + assignment (who) + scope (where: management group → subscription → resource group → resource). Deny assignments override.
Built-in roles: Owner, Contributor, Reader, User Access Administrator; plus granular ones (VM Contributor, Storage Blob Data Contributor). Data-plane vs control-plane actions differ.
Custom roles for precise needs; PIM makes admin roles eligible (just-in-time) with approval, MFA, and time limits — the privileged-access answer.
Allow/deny evaluation: explicit Deny > Allow; NotActions carve out exceptions within broad roles.

example.code:
az role assignment create --assignee prod-admins@contoso.com \
  --role 'Virtual Machine Contributor' --scope /subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/prod-rg
# eligible instead of permanent:
az rest --method PUT --url "https://management.azure.com/.../roleEligibilityScheduleRequests/..."
example.walkthrough: Assign at the narrowest scope that works. 'Admin needs occasional Owner' → PIM eligible assignment, not permanent Owner.

pitfalls: Owner at subscription scope for daily work — Contributor or narrower suffices.
Confusing control-plane (manage VM) with data-plane (read blobs) — Storage Blob Data Contributor is separate from Contributor.
Permanent admin assignments where PIM eligible would do.
lessons.try_it: Make a custom role that can restart VMs but not delete them, scoped to one resource group.

lessons.title: Privileged Identity Management (PIM)
concepts: PIM converts standing admin access into just-in-time: eligible assignments activated with MFA, approval, ticket number, and time limits.
Applies to Entra roles and Azure resource roles; access reviews periodically re-certify ('do you still need this?').
Activation alerts + audit history give the compliance trail auditors demand.
PIM requires Entra ID P2 — licensing is part of the design answer.

example.code:
# Eligible assignment: not active until requested
New-MgRoleManagementDirectoryRoleEligibilityScheduleRequest `
  -PrincipalId <user> -RoleDefinitionId <global-admin> `
  -DirectoryScopeId '/' -Action 'AdminAssign'
example.walkthrough: Zero standing privilege: admins hold eligibility, activate for 4 hours with MFA + ticket. 'Reduce blast radius of compromised admin' → PIM.

pitfalls: Leaving Global Admin permanently assigned — the exact anti-pattern PIM solves.
No access reviews — eligibility accumulates into de-facto standing access.
Forgetting P2 licensing in cost/design answers.
lessons.try_it: Configure an eligible assignment with 4-hour max duration and approval required.

lessons.title: Managed Identities: Passwordless Azure Access
concepts: System-assigned (tied to resource lifecycle) vs user-assigned (standalone, shared across resources) managed identities — no credentials to store or rotate.
The resource gets a service principal in Entra ID automatically; Azure handles token issuance via the instance metadata endpoint.
Assign RBAC roles to the identity (e.g., Key Vault Secrets User) — code just requests tokens, never sees secrets.
Federated credentials extend this to GitHub Actions/Kubernetes: OIDC trust without any stored secret.

example.code:
az vm identity assign -g prod-rg -n webvm
PRINCIPAL=$(az vm show -g prod-rg -n webvm --query identity.principalId -o tsv)
az role assignment create --assignee $PRINCIPAL \
  --role 'Key Vault Secrets User' --scope <vault-id>
# in code: DefaultAzureCredential() -- no secrets anywhere
example.walkthrough: VM identity → RBAC on Key Vault → app uses DefaultAzureCredential. Zero stored credentials. 'Eliminate secrets in code' → managed identity.

pitfalls: Storing connection strings in app settings when managed identity works — secrets sprawl.
System-assigned identity deleted with the resource — use user-assigned for shared/long-lived needs.
Forgetting RBAC on the target — identity alone grants nothing.
lessons.try_it: Give a VM identity access to a storage account and read a blob with no keys.

lessons.title: Key Vault: Secrets, Keys, and Certificates
concepts: Vaults hold secrets, keys, certificates; access via RBAC (recommended) or access policies; firewall + private endpoint for network isolation.
Managed HSM for FIPS 140-2 Level 3 dedicated hardware; soft-delete + purge protection guard against destruction.
Rotation: auto for storage keys, manual/event-grid-triggered for secrets; apps fetch at runtime via managed identity.
App Configuration for feature flags/non-secret config — separate from secrets by design.

example.code:
az keyvault secret set --vault-name prod-kv -n db-password --value '...'
az keyvault update -n prod-kv --enable-purge-protection true
# app reads via managed identity -- no secret in code
example.walkthrough: Purge protection + RBAC + private endpoint = the secure vault baseline. 'Rotate secrets safely' → versioned secrets + event grid rotation function.

pitfalls: Access policies when RBAC is the current best practice — use Azure RBAC.
No purge protection on prod vaults — accidental deletion becomes permanent.
Secrets in source control — Key Vault references in App Service/Functions instead.
lessons.try_it: Store a secret, grant an app access via managed identity, and rotate it.

lessons.title: Arc: Hybrid Machine Management
concepts: Arc projects on-prem/other-cloud servers into Azure: policy, Update Management, Defender, extensions — one control plane.
Arc-enabled Kubernetes and data services extend the model; private link scopes for secure onboarding.
Onboarding at scale: service principals + scripts; tags drive policy targeting.
Use for the 'manage everything from Azure' hybrid story.

example.code:
az connectedmachine install --resource-group rg --location eastus \
  --subscription <sub> --tags Datacenter=DC1
# then: az policy assignment, Defender enablement apply uniformly
example.walkthrough: Install agent, project into Azure, manage like native. 'Patch on-prem servers from Azure' → Arc + Update Management.

pitfalls: Agent without network planning — proxy/private-link first.
Treating Arc as migration — it is management, not migration.
No tagging strategy — policy targeting needs tags.
lessons.try_it: Onboard a test VM and apply a policy via Arc.

lessons.title: Azure Policy: Guardrails as Code
concepts: Policy definitions (if-not-compliant-then-effect) assigned at MG/subscription/RG scope; effects: Deny, Audit, Append, Modify, DeployIfNotExists.
Initiatives bundle policies (e.g., CIS benchmark); compliance dashboard shows per-assignment state; exemptions with expiry for justified exceptions.
DeployIfNotExists auto-remediates (e.g., enable Defender, add diagnostics) via a managed identity on the assignment.
Policy vs RBAC: RBAC controls who can act; Policy controls what configurations are allowed regardless of who.

example.code:
az policy assignment create --name deny-public-storage \
  --policy 'Storage account public access should be disallowed' \
  --scope /subscriptions/<sub> --enforcement-mode Default
example.walkthrough: One assignment at subscription scope blocks public storage everywhere — including admins. 'Prevent misconfiguration org-wide' → Azure Policy Deny.

pitfalls: Audit-only when you need Deny — audit finds drift, deny prevents it.
No exemptions process — teams work around policy instead of requesting justified exceptions.
Forgetting DeployIfNotExists needs a managed identity with permissions to remediate.
lessons.try_it: Assign the 'allowed locations' policy and try deploying outside it.

lessons.title: Cost Management, Tags, and Governance
concepts: Tags (owner, env, costcenter) drive chargeback; enforce via Policy (require tags, inherit from RG); locks (CanNotDelete/ReadOnly) protect critical resources.
Budgets + alerts + action groups (automation on breach); Cost Management views by tag/RG; reservations/savings plans for steady workloads.
Management groups mirror org structure for policy/RBAC inheritance; subscriptions isolate billing and blast radius.
Advisor gives cost/right-sizing/security recommendations — the exam's 'reduce spend' starting point.

example.code:
az tag create --resource-id <rg-id> --tags env=prod owner=platform costcenter=eng
az consumption budget create --budget-name eng-monthly --amount 5000 \
  --time-grain Monthly --category Cost
example.walkthrough: Tag everything → budgets per cost center → alerts at 80/100%. Untagged resources are invisible spend — Policy-enforced tagging fixes it.

pitfalls: No tagging strategy — cost attribution impossible; enforce at creation via Policy.
Budgets without action groups — alerts nobody reads; wire to automation.
Deleting prod by accident — CanNotDelete locks on critical resource groups.
lessons.try_it: Create a budget with an action group that tags over-spend resources.

lessons.title: Microsoft Defender for Cloud
concepts: CSPM: secure score, recommendations, compliance dashboards (CIS, PCI); CWPP: per-resource plans (servers, containers, SQL, storage).
Defender for Servers (P1/P2: MDE integration, file integrity, JIT VM access); Defender for Containers (registry + runtime).
Workflow automation pushes findings to action groups; regulatory compliance maps to standards automatically.
Continuous export to Log Analytics/Sentinel/Event Hub for retention and SIEM.

example.code:
az security pricing create -n VirtualMachines --tier Standard
# enable JIT instead of open RDP:
az security jit-policy create -g prod-rg --name default --vm <vm-id>
example.walkthrough: Enable plan → remediate recommendations → secure score rises. 'Just-in-time admin ports' → Defender JIT, not open NSGs.

pitfalls: Free tier expecting CWPP features — workload protections need paid plans.
Ignoring secure score recommendations — the exam treats them as required actions.
Open management ports instead of JIT — always choose JIT in design answers.
lessons.try_it: Enable Defender for Servers and remediate the top 3 recommendations.

lessons.title: Policy Initiatives and Remediation
concepts: Initiatives bundle policies (CIS, PCI, FedRAMP built-ins) into one assignment with parameters.
DeployIfNotExists/Modify effects auto-remediate; remediation tasks fix existing non-compliance.
Exemptions with expiry for accepted risk; compliance dashboard per assignment.
Policy as code: export to Bicep/Terraform, version in git.

example.code:
az policy assignment create --name cis-l1 --policy-set-definition <cis-initiative> \
  --params '{"effect": "Audit"}' --mi-system-assigned
az policy remediation create --policy-assignment <id> -g rg -n fix-existing
example.walkthrough: Assign the CIS initiative, review non-compliant, run remediation tasks. 'Enforce CIS across the estate' → initiative + remediate.

pitfalls: Deny without testing — Audit first, Deny after measuring blast radius.
No exemptions process — teams work around policy instead of through it.
Assignment sprawl — initiatives over one-off assignments.
lessons.try_it: Assign CIS L1 in Audit, remediate one resource type.

lessons.title: Blob Storage: Tiers, Lifecycle, and Access
concepts: Blob types: block (general, up to ~190TB), append (logging), page (VHDs/disks). Access tiers set at blob or account level.
Lifecycle management: tier-to-cool/cold/archive rules + delete rules; versioning keeps history; snapshots point-in-time copies.
Access: SAS tokens (scoped, expiring), stored access policies (revocable), Entra RBAC (Storage Blob Data roles), anonymous public containers.
Object replication across accounts/regions; inventory reports audit at scale.

example.code:
az storage blob generate-sas --account-name stprod001 -c reports -n q3.pdf \
  --permissions r --expiry 2026-10-11T00:00:00Z --https-only
example.walkthrough: SAS = temporary scoped access without identity. 'Share a private file for 24h' → user-delegation SAS (Entra-backed, no key exposure).

pitfalls: Account-key SAS in apps — leaks the master key; use user-delegation SAS or RBAC.
No expiry on SAS — always bound lifetime to need.
Page blobs for general files — page blobs are for VHDs; block blobs for objects.
lessons.try_it: Generate a 1-hour read-only SAS and confirm it fails after expiry.

lessons.title: Azure Files and NetApp Files
concepts: Azure Files: SMB/NFS shares in the cloud; AD/Entra Kerberos auth for lift-and-shift file servers; tiers: transaction-optimized, hot, cool.
Sync with Azure File Sync to on-prem servers (cloud tiering); snapshots + soft delete for recovery.
NetApp Files: high-performance NFS/SMB for SAP, HPC, databases — sub-ms latency, snapshots, replication.
Private endpoints keep traffic off the public internet; SMB over port 445 often blocked by ISPs — VPN/ExpressRoute or private endpoint.

example.code:
az storage share-rm create -g prod-rg --storage-account stprod001 -n dept
# mount with AD Kerberos auth (no stored keys):
net use Z: \\stprod001.file.core.windows.net\dept
example.walkthrough: Entra Kerberos auth means domain users access shares with their identity — no storage keys. 'Lift file server to cloud with AD ACLs' → Azure Files + Entra Kerberos.

pitfalls: Storage keys for user access — use Entra Kerberos/RBAC instead.
Port 445 blocked by client ISP — private endpoint or VPN required.
No backup configured — enable share snapshots or Backup vault protection.
lessons.try_it: Create a share with a snapshot policy and restore a deleted file.

lessons.title: Private Link and Private Endpoints
concepts: Private Endpoint: private IP in your VNet for PaaS (Storage, SQL, Key Vault) — traffic never leaves the Microsoft backbone.
Private Link Service: expose your own service privately to consumers; Private DNS zones resolve privatelink names.
Service endpoints are simpler but stay on public IPs with VNet identity; private endpoints are the stronger isolation.
DNS is the gotcha: on-premises needs conditional forwarders to resolve private endpoints over VPN/ER.

example.code:
az network private-endpoint create -g prod-rg -n st-pe \
  --vnet-name prod-vnet --subnet pe-subnet \
  --private-connection-resource-id <storage-id> --group-id blob \
  --connection-name st-conn
az network private-dns zone create -g prod-rg -n privatelink.blob.core.windows.net
example.walkthrough: Private endpoint + private DNS zone + VNet link = PaaS on private IPs. 'No public PaaS access' → private endpoints + disabled public network access.

pitfalls: Private endpoint without private DNS — clients resolve the public IP and fail.
Forgetting to disable public network access on the PaaS resource — endpoint alone does not close the public path.
On-prem DNS not forwarding privatelink zones — hybrid resolution breaks.
lessons.try_it: Create a private endpoint for Key Vault and resolve it from on-prem DNS.

lessons.title: Storage Mover: File Migration
concepts: Managed SMB/NFS → Azure file share migration: agents, projects, job definitions with schedules.
Copy settings: preserve ACLs/permissions; post-copy verification.
Use for file-server migrations; large block/data-lake moves use Data Box or AzCopy patterns.
Monitor via job runs; cutover after final delta sync.

example.code:
# portal/CLI: register agent -> create project -> source (SMB share) -> target (file share)
# job: migrate with 'preserve permissions', schedule nightly delta until cutover
example.walkthrough: Agent near the source, project per file server, delta syncs until cutover. 'Migrate file shares to Azure Files' → Storage Mover.

pitfalls: Cutover before final delta — data loss window.
Permissions not preserved — test ACL fidelity early.
No rollback plan — keep source until validation completes.
lessons.try_it: Migrate a test share and verify ACLs on the target.

lessons.title: Virtual Machines: Sizing, Disks, and Availability
concepts: Sizes: B (burstable), D (general), E (memory), F (compute), N (network), NV (GPU). Pick family first, then size — right-sizing via Advisor.
Disks: OS + data; Premium SSD v2 (sub-ms, independent IOPS), Premium SSD, Standard SSD, Ultra Disk (top perf, regional constraints).
Availability: single VM (99.9% premium SSD), Availability Set (FD+UD, 99.95%), Availability Zones (99.99%), VMSS for scale.
Ephemeral OS disks for stateless (faster, cheaper); managed disks for everything; disk encryption with platform or customer keys.

example.code:
az vm create -g prod-rg -n web1 --image Ubuntu2204 \
  --size Standard_D2s_v5 --vnet-name prod-vnet --subnet app \
  --zone 1 --os-disk-size-gb 64 --storage-sku PremiumV2_LRS \
  --assign-identity --nsg web-nsg
example.walkthrough: Zone-pinned, managed identity, right NSG, premium disk. Exam pattern: '99.99% for VMs' → zone-redundant deployment across 3 zones.

pitfalls: Single VM expecting HA — SLA requires sets/zones; design accordingly.
Oversized VMs 'just in case' — Advisor right-sizing cuts 30-50% routinely.
Unmanaged disks in new designs — always managed disks.
lessons.try_it: Deploy 2 VMs across zones behind a load balancer and test zone failure.

lessons.title: VM Scale Sets: Autoscaling Fleets
concepts: VMSS = identical VMs from one image, autoscaled by metrics/schedules, with rolling upgrades and automatic repairs.
Uniform vs Flexible orchestration: flexible adds per-VM control, mixed SKUs, and FD spread like availability sets.
Autoscale rules on CPU/queue length/custom metrics; scale-in protection for stateful instances; scheduled profiles for known patterns.
Pair with Application Gateway or Load Balancer; health extension reports app-level health for auto-repair.

example.code:
az vmss create -g prod-rg -n webss --image Ubuntu2204 \
  --vm-sku Standard_D2s_v5 --instance-count 2 --zones 1 2 3 \
  --lb web-lb --health-probe app-health --upgrade-policy-mode Rolling
example.walkthrough: Zones 1-2-3 + rolling upgrades + health-based repair = self-healing fleet. 'Handle variable web traffic' → VMSS + autoscale rules.

pitfalls: No health probe — broken instances stay in rotation; app-health extension fixes it.
Manual upgrades on 100 VMs — rolling upgrade policy automates safely.
Autoscale on CPU for queue-driven work — scale on queue length instead.
lessons.try_it: Configure autoscale: out at 70% CPU, in at 30%, with 5-min cooldown.

lessons.title: Automation Accounts: Runbooks
concepts: Runbooks (PowerShell/Python) for scheduled/triggered ops: patching, cleanup, start/stop schedules; Hybrid Workers for on-prem.
Update Management Center (successor to Update Management) patches Azure + Arc machines.
Source control integration; webhooks trigger runbooks from alerts.
Managed identities on runbooks — no stored credentials.

example.code:
# Start/Stop VM runbook (scheduled):
Connect-AzAccount -Identity
Stop-AzVM -ResourceGroupName $rg -Name $vm -Force  # nights/weekends
example.walkthrough: Schedule the runbook; managed identity handles auth. 'Stop dev VMs at night' → Automation runbook on a schedule.

pitfalls: Stored credentials in runbooks — managed identity instead.
No error handling/notifications — silent failures in scheduled ops.
Hybrid Worker unpatched — the worker itself needs maintenance.
lessons.try_it: Schedule a runbook that stops a dev VM at 8pm.

lessons.title: Virtual Networks: Addressing and Subnets
concepts: VNets are regional: address space (e.g., 10.0.0.0/16), subnets per purpose; first 4 + last 1 IPs reserved per subnet.
Peering connects VNets (same/different regions) with low latency; non-transitive — hub-spoke via hub VNet or Virtual WAN.
Service endpoints extend VNet identity to PaaS; private endpoints give PaaS a private IP in your VNet — the secure pattern.
Plan non-overlapping ranges for peering/VPN; use /16 per VNet with /24 subnets as a starting convention.

example.code:
az network vnet create -g prod-rg -n prod-vnet --address-prefix 10.0.0.0/16
az network vnet subnet create -g prod-rg --vnet-name prod-vnet -n app --address-prefix 10.0.1.0/24
az network vnet subnet create -g prod-rg --vnet-name prod-vnet -n data --address-prefix 10.0.2.0/24
example.walkthrough: App/data/db tiers as subnets; NSGs per tier. 'Isolate tiers' → subnets + NSGs; 'connect VNets' → peering.

pitfalls: Overlapping address spaces then needing peering — re-addressing is painful; plan upfront.
Expecting transitive peering — A↔B and B↔C does not give A↔C; use hub-spoke.
Public endpoints on PaaS when private endpoints were required — exam security trap.
lessons.try_it: Peer two VNets and verify non-transitivity with a third.

lessons.title: NSGs, ASGs, and Traffic Filtering
concepts: NSGs: 5-tuple rules (source/dest, port, protocol), processed lowest-number-first; default deny inbound, allow outbound/VNet.
Apply at subnet and/or NIC; effective rules are the union; flow logs (to Log Analytics/Storage) record accepts/denies.
Application Security Groups (ASGs) let rules reference workload roles ('web', 'db') instead of IPs — rules survive re-IPing.
NACL-equivalent stateless filtering does not exist in Azure — NSGs are stateful; use Azure Firewall for L7/deny rules.

example.code:
az network nsg rule create -g prod-rg --nsg-name db-nsg -n allow-sql \
  --priority 100 --source-asgs web-asg --destination-port-ranges 1433 \
  --destination-asgs db-asg --access Allow --protocol Tcp
example.walkthrough: ASG-to-ASG rule: web tier → SQL on 1433, no hardcoded IPs. 'Microsegment by role' → ASGs in NSG rules.

pitfalls: Allow 0.0.0.0/0 to RDP/SSH — the most flagged misconfiguration; use Bastion + JIT.
Rule priority confusion — lower number wins; a broad allow at 100 shadows a deny at 200.
No flow logs — you cannot troubleshoot what you cannot see.
lessons.try_it: Enable flow logs and find the denied connection in Log Analytics.

lessons.title: Load Balancing: LB, App Gateway, Front Door
concepts: Load Balancer (L4): public/internal, SKU standard (zone-redundant), backend pools, health probes, NAT rules; source-IP affinity option.
Application Gateway (L7): WAF, path/host routing, TLS termination, autoscaling v2 SKU; AGIC integrates with AKS.
Front Door (global L7): anycast edge, instant failover, WAF, Private Link to origins; Traffic Manager is DNS-level (no proxy).
Decision: regional L4 → LB; regional L7+WAF → App GW; global → Front Door; DNS-only → Traffic Manager.

example.code:
az network lb create -g prod-rg -n web-lb --sku Standard --public-ip-zone 1
az network lb probe create -g prod-rg --lb-name web-lb -n http-probe \
  --protocol http --port 80 --path /health
example.walkthrough: Health probe path must return 200 — same trap as AWS. Global app? Front Door in front of regional App Gateways is the reference architecture.

pitfalls: Basic SKU LB for production — no SLA/zones; Standard is required.
Front Door without WAF on public apps — edge protection belongs at the edge.
Expecting Traffic Manager to proxy — it is DNS only; failover speed depends on TTL.
lessons.try_it: Put Front Door in front of two regional App Gateways and test failover.

lessons.title: Azure DNS: Public, Private, and Hybrid
concepts: Public DNS zones host internet records (alias A for Azure resources); private DNS zones resolve VNet-internal names, linked to VNets.
Private resolver (inbound/outbound endpoints) bridges on-prem DNS and Azure private zones over VPN/ER.
Traffic Manager profiles (priority/weighted/performance/geographic) steer DNS-level traffic; Front Door is the proxy alternative.
DNSSEC not natively supported on Azure DNS — know the limitation for exam questions.

example.code:
az network private-dns zone create -g prod-rg -n corp.internal
az network private-dns link vnet create -g prod-rg -z corp.internal \
  -n prod-link --virtual-network prod-vnet --registration-enabled true
example.walkthrough: Auto-registration: VMs register corp.internal names automatically. 'Internal name resolution' → private DNS zone + VNet link.

pitfalls: Expecting DNSSEC on Azure DNS — not supported; note it as a limitation.
No VNet link on the private zone — records exist but nobody resolves them.
Using Traffic Manager for instant failover — DNS TTL governs; Front Door is faster.
lessons.try_it: Link a private zone with auto-registration and resolve a VM by short name.

lessons.title: Azure Firewall: Managed Network Security
concepts: Managed stateful firewall: DNAT, network rules, application rules (FQDN), TLS inspection (Premium).
Premium: IDPS signatures, URL filtering, TLS inspection; Standard: L3-L7 filtering with threat intel.
Firewall Policy hierarchy: base + child policies for hub-and-spoke governance.
Forced tunneling and multiple public IPs for SNAT scale.

example.code:
az network firewall create -g rg -n fw --sku AZFW_VNet
az network firewall policy create -g rg -n fwpol --sku Premium
# application rule: allow *.windowsupdate.com for patching
example.walkthrough: Spoke traffic routes to the hub firewall; policies control egress by FQDN. 'Control all outbound traffic' → Azure Firewall.

pitfalls: Allowing 0.0.0.0/0 outbound — the firewall exists to stop that.
No TLS inspection cert — encrypted C2 channels pass blind.
SNAT exhaustion — add public IPs for large spoke counts.
lessons.try_it: Write an FQDN allow-rule for updates and deny everything else.

lessons.title: Bastion: Secure VM Access
concepts: Fully managed RDP/SSH via portal — no public IPs, no jump boxes, no NSG holes.
Standard SKU: IP-based connection, file copy, session recording, shareable links.
Deployed to AzureBastionSubnet (/26+); one per VNet (or shared via peering).
Session recording aids compliance for privileged access.

example.code:
az network bastion create -g rg -n bastion --vnet-name vnet \
  --public-ip-address bastion-pip --location eastus --sku Standard
example.walkthrough: Deploy to the dedicated subnet; connect from the portal with AAD credentials. 'RDP without public IPs' → Bastion.

pitfalls: Subnet too small — AzureBastionSubnet needs /26 or larger.
Public IPs on VMs 'temporarily' — Bastion removes the excuse.
Basic SKU when recording needed — Standard adds the compliance features.
lessons.try_it: Connect via Bastion and verify no public IP on the VM.

lessons.title: Microsoft Sentinel: Cloud SIEM/SOAR
concepts: Sentinel ingests via data connectors (Entra, Defender, firewalls); analytics rules (scheduled/NRT/ML/fusion) create incidents.
Fusion correlates low-fidelity signals into high-fidelity incidents; UEBA baselines entity behavior; watchlists enrich.
SOAR: playbooks (Logic Apps) auto-respond — isolate VM, revoke sessions, open tickets; automation rules triage.
Hunting queries proactively search; MITRE ATT&CK mapping shows coverage gaps.

example.code:
// Hunting: impossible travel
SigninLogs
| where ResultType == 0
| summarize locations=dcount(Location), ips=make_set(IPAddress) by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)

lessons.title: KQL for Log Analytics

Performance: filter early (TimeGenerated first), project only needed columns, avoid * in production queries.

| summarize failures=count() by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| where failures > 5
| order by failures desc

One-off queries for repeat detections — save as functions/alerts.

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: The study order is deliberate — follow it: Start Here (this domain: how to study, Azure Administrator exam structure) → Lessons (deep-dives in domain order: Entra ID & Identity, Governance & Compliance, Storage, Compute (VMs), Virtual Networking, Monitoring) → Scenarios (multiple-choice drills, untimed, with full explanations) → Labs (hands-on terminal exercises) → Timed mock (the full AZ-104 simulation). Each layer assumes the one before.

What 'terminal' means: a terminal (also called console or shell) is a text window where you type commands and the computer prints results — no buttons, no mouse. Cloud CLIs (aws, az) follow the same pattern: service, then action, then flags. You cannot break anything by typing a wrong command in the labs — the worst case is an error message, which is itself information.

The AZ-104 exam strategy baked into this bootcamp: learn the concept in Lessons, recognize it in Scenarios, execute it in Labs, then prove it under time pressure in the Mock. Skipping straight to the mock is like taking the final before the lectures.

How to read the drills: every scenario has a 'why' explanation naming the correct answer's letter. Wrong answers are designed around real misconceptions — read every explanation, especially for questions you got right by guessing.

example.code:
Week 1-2: Start Here + first 3 domains (lessons + scenarios)
Week 3-4: remaining domains + all labs
Week 5:   exam-strategy domain + timed mock runs
Exam day:  light review of pitfalls only — no new material

Suggested pace: 80-100 hours of focused study. Two 90-minute sessions beat one 3-hour slog.
example.walkthrough: Timebox each domain: lessons one day, scenarios the next, labs the third. The mock at the end measures readiness — 80%+ twice in a row means book the exam.

pitfalls: Binge-reading lessons without doing scenarios — recognition is a different skill from recall; the exam tests recognition under pressure.
Skipping labs because 'I know the CLI' — muscle memory fails under exam stress; the labs build it.
Taking the mock once, scoring 65%, and booking the exam anyway — the mock is a gate, not a suggestion.

lessons.title: AZ-104 Exam Structure and Question Patterns
concepts: The AZ-104 exam is multiple-choice and multiple-response, delivered at a testing center or via online proctoring. Questions are scenario-based: a paragraph of context, then 'what should you do?' — never pure trivia.

Every question has one best answer and three distractors built from common misconceptions. Two answers often look right; the correct one matches the constraint words: 'most cost-effective,' 'least operational overhead,' 'most secure,' 'highly available.'
Microsoft exams test decision-making, not memorization: expect 'a company needs X with constraints Y and Z' and four architectures. Your job is to map constraints to services.
Flag-and-return: answer what you know fast, flag the hard ones, return with remaining time. Unanswered questions score zero — never leave blanks.

example.code:
Question anatomy:
  Stem: 'A company runs ... The solution must be highly available
         and minimize operational overhead. What should the architect do?'
  Constraint words: HIGHLY AVAILABLE + MINIMIZE OPERATIONAL OVERHEAD
  -> eliminate self-managed options (operational overhead)
  -> eliminate single-AZ options (availability)
  -> pick the managed multi-AZ answer
example.walkthrough: Underline constraint words first, eliminate two distractors, then choose between the last two by re-reading the stem. This mechanical process beats 'gut feeling' consistently.

pitfalls: Answering from real-world habit instead of the exam's best practice — the exam wants the textbook answer, not your team's workaround.
Ignoring constraint words — 'cheapest' vs 'most resilient' flip the correct answer between the same two options.
Changing answers on review without new reasoning — first instincts, backed by elimination, are usually right.
lessons.try_it: Take 5 scenarios in the drills and write down the constraint words before answering.

lessons.title: Hands-On Labs: Building Muscle Memory
concepts: Labs are terminal exercises with automated checks: each step gives you a command to run, and checks verify the result. A hint appears if a check fails — read it, it diagnoses the exact miss.
The lab terminal is a safe sandbox: create, delete, break things. Every exam objective you can DO is one you will not forget under pressure.

For Azure Administrator, the highest-value lab skills are the ones questions describe as actions: creating, configuring, verifying, troubleshooting. If a scenario says 'the engineer runs X,' you should have run X in a lab.
Repeat labs you fumble. The second run should take half the time — that speed delta is exam readiness.

example.code:
Lab loop:
  1. Read the objective (what 'done' looks like)
  2. Run each step, observing output (not just copy-paste)
  3. If a check fails, read the hint -- it names the exact gap
  4. Finish, then re-do the lab from memory tomorrow

  Checks are your examiner: green means you actually did it.
example.walkthrough: Do not copy-paste blindly: after each command, ask 'what did that change?' The checks only pass when the real state is correct.

pitfalls: Copy-pasting without reading output — the exam will ask what the output means.
Skipping the failed-check hints — they are the fastest diagnosis you will get anywhere.
Doing each lab once — spaced repetition (day 1, day 3, day 7) locks it in.
lessons.try_it: Complete any lab in the first domain, then redo it tomorrow without looking.

lessons.title: Study Plan and Readiness Gates

Phase 2 — Hands-on (weeks 3-4): all labs + remaining domains. Gate: every lab completed without hints.
Phase 3 — Pressure (week 5): exam-strategy domain, then full mock runs. Gate: two consecutive mock scores at or above 80%.
The two-mock rule is non-negotiable: one good score is luck, two is readiness. Book the exam only after clearing it.

lessons.title: Capstone: Hub-Spoke Landing Zone — Plan
concepts: Your capstone proves Azure Administrator skills end-to-end: a production landing zone: hub VNet with VPN gateway and Firewall, peered spokes, private endpoints everywhere, Entra ID with PIM, Policy guardrails, and backup
Plan before building: define success criteria (what 'done' looks like), list every service/resource, and sequence the build so each step is verifiable.
Document as you go: architecture diagram, decisions and tradeoffs, costs. Hiring managers and examiners both grade the trail, not just the result.
Scope control: the capstone must be finishable in a weekend. Cut nice-to-haves ruthlessly; depth on core objectives beats breadth.

  Milestone 2: Network: hub-spoke VNets, VPN gateway, Azure Firewall, private endpoints for storage/key vault

example.walkthrough: Write the milestones on paper first. Each milestone ends with a verification command — if you cannot verify it, it is not done.

pitfalls: Building without milestones — 'almost done' for three weeks is not done.
No cost estimate — surprise bills kill momentum; estimate first.

lessons.title: Reading Questions Like an Examiner
concepts: Examiners write distractors from real mistakes: the 'almost right' answer that misses one constraint, the 'real-world habit' answer that is not best practice, the 'correct service, wrong feature' answer.
Constraint words decide everything: 'MOST cost-effective,' 'LEAST operational overhead,' 'MOST secure,' 'WITHOUT managing servers,' 'MEET compliance.' Circle them before reading options.
Length is a signal, not noise: long stems hide the one sentence that matters. Read the last sentence first (the actual question), then scan for constraints.
Absolute words ('always,' 'never') are usually wrong; qualified words ('typically,' 'minimize') usually right — but verify against constraints, never as a sole rule.

example.code:
Stem: '...must retain logs for 7 years for compliance, with minimal
 effort. What is the MOST cost-effective solution?'
Parse: constraint = 7-YEAR RETENTION + MINIMAL EFFORT + CHEAPEST
Eliminate: manual pipelines (effort), hot storage for 7 years (cost)
Answer family: lifecycle to archive tier + retention policy
example.walkthrough: Practice this parse on every drill: constraints → eliminate two → decide between two. Speed comes from the mechanical habit.

pitfalls: Reading options before the stem — anchors you to attractive distractors.
Choosing the 'coolest' service instead of the constrained one — exam rewards boring and correct.
Overthinking 'trick' questions — most are straightforward constraint matches.
lessons.try_it: Do 10 scenarios writing only the constraint words first; check if your accuracy rises.

lessons.title: Elimination Tactics That Work
concepts: Two-pass method: pass 1 eliminates options violating any constraint (usually kills 2); pass 2 compares survivors on the remaining constraints.
Service-family elimination: if the stem needs serverless, eliminate every EC2/VM-based option immediately without reading further.
Cost-order elimination: when 'most cost-effective' appears, rank options by managed-ness — more managed usually wins unless a constraint forbids it.
Security-order elimination: when 'most secure,' prefer options with encryption by default, private networking, and least privilege — in that order.

example.code:
Q: '...serverless, lowest cost, event-driven image processing...'
A) EC2 fleet with cron        -> eliminate (not serverless)
B) Lambda + S3 events        -> keep
C) ECS on EC2                -> eliminate (not serverless)
D) Lambda + polling EC2      -> eliminate (polling = waste)
Answer: B in under 20 seconds.
example.walkthrough: Elimination turns 4-option questions into 2-option questions, doubling your odds even when unsure. Drill it until it is reflex.

pitfalls: Eliminating on vibes — every elimination needs a cited constraint from the stem.
Keeping an option because it 'sounds enterprise' — the exam does not grade vibes.
Forgetting to re-read the stem after elimination — the final two need the full context.
lessons.try_it: For the next 15 scenarios, write your two eliminations and reasons before choosing.

lessons.title: Time Management Under Pressure
concepts: Budget per question: total minutes ÷ question count, minus 15 minutes buffer. For a 130-minute, 65-question AZ-104: ~1m45s each. A 3-minute question is stealing from two others.
The 90-second rule: if you have not eliminated two options in 90 seconds, flag and move on. Hard questions cluster — do not let one sink your pace.
First pass: answer everything you can in under 60 seconds. Second pass: flagged questions with fresh eyes. Third pass: review marked-for-review only.
Never leave blanks: with no penalty for wrong answers, a guess among two survivors is a 50% expected score vs 0% blank.

example.code:
65 questions, 130 minutes:
  Pass 1 (60 min): all sub-60s questions -> ~40 answered
  Pass 2 (40 min): flagged questions -> ~20 answered
  Pass 3 (15 min): review marked -> adjust a few
  Buffer (15 min):  breathing room / technical issues
example.walkthrough: Practice with the mock timer. Your pass-1 speed is the skill — the mock's per-question pacing feedback trains exactly this.

pitfalls: Perfectionism on question 7 — the exam is won on questions 30-65, which you never reach.
No flagging discipline — 'I'll remember to come back' fails under stress; flag explicitly.
Skipping the buffer — technical hiccups happen; plan for them.
lessons.try_it: Run a 20-question drill with a 35-minute timer and enforce the 90-second rule.

lessons.title: Scenario Questions: Multi-Service Design
concepts: Hard questions combine 2-3 services: identify each requirement, map it to a service, then check the combination for conflicts (regions, limits, auth).
Draw the data flow: source → processing → storage → consumer. Wrong answers usually break one arrow (wrong trigger, wrong permission, wrong region).
Permissions are the hidden test: the architecture can be perfect and still wrong if the role/policy is missing. Always ask 'who is allowed to call what?'
Cost and operations are tiebreakers: between two working designs, the exam prefers managed, serverless, and event-driven.

example.code:
Flow check for 'S3 upload -> process -> notify':
  S3 event notification -> Lambda? (permission: s3:Put -> lambda:Invoke?)
  Lambda -> DynamoDB? (execution role allows dynamodb:PutItem?)
  Lambda -> SNS? (role allows sns:Publish?)
  Dead-letter on failure? (SQS DLQ configured?)
  => 4 arrows, 4 permission checks. The distractor breaks exactly one.
example.walkthrough: For every design question, sketch the arrows and label the permission on each. The option with all arrows green is the answer.

pitfalls: Checking services but not permissions — the exam's favorite trap.
Forgetting DLQs/retries on async flows — 'what happens on failure' is always asked.
Regional mismatch — KMS keys, some services, and data residency are regional.
lessons.try_it: Take any 3-service scenario and draw the arrow diagram with permissions labeled.

simulations.title: The VM that billed while stopped
simulations.brief: Finance asks why ilb-web-01 still bills after being 'stopped' all month. The portal shows 'Stopped' — not 'Stopped (deallocated)'. Investigate.

steps.symptom: A 'stopped' VM still incurs compute charges.
options: The VM was stopped but not deallocated — deallocate it to stop compute billing

It is normal — stopped VMs always bill full compute
steps.explain: In Azure, 'Stopped' keeps the VM allocated on the host (and billing); 'Stopped (deallocated)' releases it. az vm stop deallocates — but a portal Stop without deallocate does not. The state string tells the story.

simulations.debrief: You learned the AZ-104 billing trap: stopped is not deallocated. Always verify the deallocated state before promising savings.

choices.label: Approve the key — it is the fastest path

simulations.title: The NSG that blocks the app
simulations.brief: The app team says the new NSG 'broke everything'. Review the rules and click the lines causing the outage.

steps.config:
nsg-ilb-app inbound:
1. priority 100: deny 0.0.0.0/0 -> *
2. priority 200: allow 10.0.1.0/24 -> 443
3. priority 300: allow AzureLoadBalancer -> *
4. priority 400: allow 10.0.0.0/8 -> 22

issues.description: A priority-100 deny-all sits above every allow rule — NSGs evaluate lowest priority number first, so nothing after line 1 is ever reached.
issues.fix: Move the deny-all to the highest priority number (evaluated last) or remove it; default deny already exists.

issues.description: SSH open to the entire 10.0.0.0/8 is far broader than the admin jump range the ticket specified.

simulations.debrief: You caught the NSG priority trap: the lowest number wins, so a top deny-all silences every allow below it. Order is the whole game in NSGs.

sections.heading: Entra ID & Identity
items: SSPR — SSPR lets users reset their own passwords after verifying via registered authentication methods (Microsoft Authenticator, phone, etc.).
Authentication methods — it requires the methods be registered in advance and SSPR enabled for the users — the classic help-desk ticket reducer.

Dynamic — Dynamic groups evaluate membership rules against user attributes automatically — new hires with department=Sales join instantly, departures leave. Combined with dynamic groups, onboarding becomes zero-touch.

B2B collaboration — entra B2B lets external users authenticate with their own identity (even a Gmail-backed account) as guests, with access scoped to specific resources and governed by Conditional Access and access reviews.
Guest access — conditional Access evaluates signals (user/group, location, device, sign-in risk from Identity Protection) and enforces grants like require MFA or block.
Common trap — conditional Access without any MFA grant.
Common trap — a Conditional Access policy blocking legacy auth.
Common trap — a Conditional Access policy per user.
Common trap — assigning licenses via Conditional Access.

Conditional Access — Conditional Access evaluates signals (user/group, location, device, sign-in risk from Identity Protection) and enforces grants like require MFA or block. Risk-based policies are the standard response to impossible-travel and leaked-credential signals.

sections.heading: Governance & Compliance
items: RBAC follows least privilege — grant the smallest role at the narrowest scope that still lets the person work. Custom roles define exact allowed actions (Actions/NotActions/DataActions) when built-in roles are too broad or too narrow.
RBAC definition — azure Policy's built-in 'Allowed locations' definition with deny effect blocks non-compliant deployments at creation time and flags existing ones as non-compliant.

Azure Policy — Azure Policy's tag requirements (built-in 'Require a tag and its value') can deny untagged deployments or append the tag via modify, and the compliance dashboard lists every non-compliant resource for cleanup.
Deny — Deny only stops new deployments; remediation fixes the past.
Common trap — no locks; use RBAC Reader instead.
Common trap — an RBAC role called Tag Contributor.
Common trap — remove all roles and use shared admin credentials.
Common trap — keep Contributor but add a resource lock.

Read — Read the setup and name the principle at play before looking at the reasoning. Then compare your answer with the takeaway — if they differ, re-read the concepts above and try the drill scenarios for this domain.

sections.heading: Storage
items: Storage redundancy — the storage account firewall (Firewalls and virtual networks) defaults to deny and whitelists VNets (via service endpoints/private endpoints) and IP ranges. Storage Explorer is fine for small interactive work but not 10 TB bulk migration.
ZRS — ZRS synchronously replicates three copies across availability zones in the primary region — surviving a datacenter loss without paying for a second region.
Access tiers — shared access signatures grant constrained, time-limited access (permissions, IP, expiry) without exposing account keys.
Lifecycle management policies automate tier transitions by age — e.g., Hot→Cool after 30 days, →Archive after 180 — so nobody does it manually.
Least-privilege access — a service SAS on the container with write-only for 48 hours is the least-privilege answer; keys and RBAC are far too broad.
Common trap — enable soft delete instead.
Common trap — the storage account key emailed to the partner.
Common trap — azure Storage Explorer for 10 TB bulk loads.
Common trap — az PowerShell New-AzStorageBlob one file at a time.

AzCopy — is the purpose-built high-performance copy tool (azcopy copy/sync), multi-threaded with automatic resume on failure. Storage Explorer is fine for small interactive work but not 10 TB bulk migration.

sections.heading: Compute (VMs)
items: Series selection — VM series encode their optimization: F = compute, E/D = memory (E has higher memory-to-CPU), L = storage, N = GPU.
VM SLA — azure's SLA for VMs reaches 99.99% with two or more instances across availability zones.
Availability sets — provide fault/update domain spread but no scaling or identical-image management.
Scale sets — managed disk performance (IOPS and MB/s) is determined by disk type and size: Premium SSD tiers scale with provisioned size, Ultra Disk allows independent tuning.
Autoscale — VMSS manages identical VMs as a set with autoscale based on metrics (CPU, queue length), plus rolling upgrades.
Common trap — all VM series are identical; the app needs more disks.
Common trap — a VPN gateway for every admin laptop.
Common trap — enable page file on the temp disk.
Common trap — the VM needs an availability set, not a resize.

sections.heading: Virtual Networking
items: Rule priority — NSG rules are processed in priority order, lowest number first; the first match decides.

VNet peering — a-to-C needs its own peering (or a hub VNet with routing/NVA). Private endpoints bring the PaaS service into your VNet with a private IP (resolving via private DNS zone), eliminating public endpoint exposure.
ExpressRoute vs VPN — S2S VPN rides the public internet with variable throughput; peering only connects Azure VNets.
Common trap — peering requires identical address spaces.
Common trap — vNet peering to the on-premises network.
Common trap — create a private endpoint for DNS.
Common trap — priority numbers are ignored for inbound rules.

Private — Private endpoints bring the PaaS service into your VNet with a private IP (resolving via private DNS zone), eliminating public endpoint exposure. Service endpoints extend VNet identity to the service but the public endpoint remains.

sections.heading: Monitoring
items: Metrics — are lightweight numeric time-series (great for charts and metric alerts); logs are rich records stored in Log Analytics workspaces and queried with KQL (great for forensic search). Metric alert rules evaluate platform/guest metrics on a frequency and fire a…
